overview: Chorus is New Zealand's largest fixed-line telecommunications infrastructure company, built through the government-backed Ultra-Fast Broadband (UFB) public-private partnership completed in the early-to-mid 2020s. It operates a wholesale-only, open-access fibre (and shrinking legacy copper) network covering roughly 84% of New Zealand's fibre footprint (the rest served by three smaller Local Fibre Companies), selling connectivity to around 90 retail service providers (Spark, One NZ/Vodafone, 2degrees, and smaller ISPs) rather than to end consumers directly. As a regulated natural monopoly, Chorus' fibre revenues, allowed returns and capital spend are set by the Commerce Commission under a Price-Quality Path (PQ) building-blocks/RAB regime, with the second regulatory period (PQ2) running 1 January 2025 to 31 December 2028.

business_model.summary: Chorus earns regulated, largely fixed monthly wholesale access fees from retail service providers for fibre (GPON/P2P) and legacy copper connections. Revenue is highly recurring (subscription-like wholesale access charges) with a growing high-speed/high-ARPU mix as customers upgrade plans and migrate off declining copper. The completed UFB build means capital expenditure has stepped down from build-era peaks (~$650-670m p.a.) toward a sustaining/growth capex base of roughly $375-415m p.a. (FY26 guidance, expected to land in the lower half), turning Chorus into a free-cash-flow-generative, high-payout infrastructure/income stock.
business_model.customer_type: B2B wholesale-only; sells to ~90 retail service providers (Spark, One NZ, 2degrees, and smaller ISPs) who in turn serve NZ residential and business end customers. Chorus has no direct retail relationship or brand-facing role with consumers.
business_model.geographic_mix: 100% New Zealand. Nationwide fixed-line network with 1.129 million fibre connections (95% of the 1.192 million total fixed-line connections at 31 December 2025) and rapidly declining copper, covering most of the country outside three Local Fibre Company (LFC) regions (Enable/Christchurch, Northpower/Whangarei, Tuatahi First Fibre/Waikato rural).

main_competitors: Starlink and other LEO satellite broadband
competitive_position.market_position: Regulated monopoly wholesaler across ~84% of the UFB fibre footprint (the remainder split among three smaller Local Fibre Companies under the same PQ regulatory framework); no fibre-on-fibre overbuild competition within its own footprint, but faces inter-technology competition (FWA, satellite) for connections, especially in rural/low-density areas and at the low end of the market.

moat_factors.factor: Regulated natural monopoly / high barriers to entry
moat_factors.description: Duplicating a nationwide fibre network is capital-prohibitive; Chorus is the default wholesale fibre provider across most of NZ with Commerce Commission-set, cost-recovery-based revenue via the RAB, giving highly visible, government-sanctioned cash flows.

moat_factors.factor: Essential-service switching costs at the wholesale layer
moat_factors.description: Retail service providers are effectively captive to whichever network passes a given address; end customers rarely have a same-cost, same-speed fixed alternative to fibre once available, and fibre is increasingly viewed as an essential utility (34% half-on-half increase in reconnections of previously-disconnected customers noted in HY26).

PQ2 (2025-2028) sets allowed revenue off a RAB split into a Core RAB and a Financial Loss Asset that rolls forward with approved capex and an allowed WACC, giving multi-year revenue/cash-flow visibility uncommon among industrials. Exact current RAB value and allowed WACC were not separately quantified in the extracted filings reviewed; the HY26 report notes CY25 RAB capex allocations are unaudited pending the Information Disclosure announcement due in May 2026 -- treat any precise RAB/WACC figure as needing confirmation from that disclosure or the Commerce Commission's PQ2 final determination.

moat_factors.factor: Network scale and cost position vs FWA/satellite
moat_factors.description: Fibre offers materially higher speed, lower latency, and better reliability/economics per GB than 5G FWA or LEO satellite at high usage levels, supporting continued uptake growth even as those technologies erode the addressable market at the margin.

weaknesses: Zero pricing power outside the regulator-approved framework — Chorus cannot raise prices or reallocate capital freely; upside is capped by regulatory determinations

Structural decline of copper revenue as customers migrate to fibre or alternative technologies; copper connections fell from 132,000 at 31 Dec 2024 to roughly 63,000 at 30 June 2025 to 63,000/53,000 range and toward ~3,000 remaining in fibre zones by early 2026, requiring active cost/asset management (and accelerated depreciation) to retire the legacy network profitably
No brand or direct customer relationship — entirely dependent on retail service providers' marketing, pricing and bundling decisions to drive connections and ARPU

High leverage (net debt/EBITDA circa 4.5x) built up during the UFB build years constrains discretionary capital allocation and dividend flexibility if rates or EBITDA disappoint; total equity has fallen to $430m (from $567m at 30 June 2025 and $841m at 1 July 2024) against total debt (current + non-current) of roughly $3.34bn at 31 December 2025
Mature-market ceiling: uptake in NZ's largest cities is already well above 70%, with the marginal connections increasingly rural, contested (FWA/Starlink) or low-value

growth_drivers: Continued fibre uptake growth toward management's 80% target by 2030 (from 72.4% at HY26), adding high-margin incremental connections onto an already-built network

ARPU growth from plan mix-shift to higher speed tiers (gigabit/multi-gigabit steady at ~25% of the base) and CPI/inflation-linked regulated price increases (January 2025 price rise lifted fibre ARPU from $55.34 to $57.73 per month over the year to December 2025)

Copper withdrawal programme cutting network maintenance, electricity and operating costs as the legacy network is decommissioned; the Commerce Commission's 2025 draft/final recommendation to deregulate copper access services let Chorus bring forward full copper retirement to 2028, two years earlier than the prior 2030 target, directly improving EBITDA margin sooner than previously modelled

Post-UFB capex step-down (from ~$650-670m p.a. build-era peak toward ~$375-415m p.a. FY26 guided sustaining/growth capex, tracking to the lower half of that range) mechanically expanding free cash flow available for dividends

New/adjacent revenue lines: Edge Centre co-location, smart-location/IoT connectivity, dark fibre/backhaul for cellsites and data centres (the Trans-Tasman Ring project was shelved in FY26/HY26 and is no longer being actively pursued)
PQ2 regulatory settlement (2025-2028) providing multi-year revenue and capex allowance certainty, supporting the higher (70-90% of net operating FCF) dividend payout policy set in FY24

Commerce Commission deregulation of copper services outside fibre areas (recommended 2025 on the view that FWA/satellite competition has made copper regulation unnecessary) removing compliance costs and TSO-style obligations for the shrinking rural copper footprint faster than expected

business.risk: Fixed wireless access (FWA) and satellite (Starlink) competition
business.description: New Zealand has among the OECD's highest per-capita satellite broadband and FWA uptake; low-usage and price-sensitive/rural customers increasingly bypass fibre entirely, capping the uptake ceiling and pressuring low-end ARPU. The Commerce Commission itself cited this substitution as the basis for recommending copper deregulation.

Uptake is already >70% in Chorus' footprint; each incremental point of uptake becomes harder to win as remaining prospects are disproportionately price-sensitive, rural, or already served by an alternative technology.

business.risk: Retail service provider concentration and behaviour
business.description: Chorus has no direct end-customer relationship; volume and ARPU depend on Spark, One NZ and 2degrees' retail pricing, bundling and marketing choices.

Managing the now-accelerated decommissioning of a legacy network (customer migration, remaining TSO/regulatory obligations, asset write-offs, further accelerated depreciation) by the new 2028 target while maintaining service levels carries operational and reputational risk.

financial.risk: High leverage relative to a regulated-utility peer group
financial.description: Net debt/EBITDA of roughly 4.5x at HY26 (31 December 2025), close to Chorus' internal 4.75x policy tolerance and the ~5.0x threshold typically cited by rating agencies, leaves limited headroom for discretionary investment or a downside EBITDA/rate shock. Total equity of $430m against total liabilities of $5.7bn underscores the thin cushion.

Total debt of roughly $3.34bn (current $113m + non-current $3,223m) including EUR and AUD medium-term notes swapped back to NZD; weighted average interest rate was 4.9% in HY26 (down from 5.7% in HY25, with ~70% of floating exposure hedged), but large maturities recur through 2032, and higher-for-longer global rates would raise refinancing costs and pressure the payout ratio.

Substantial EUR (EMTN) and AUD (AMTN) debt requires cross-currency interest rate swaps; while fully hedged by policy, this adds counterparty and hedge-effectiveness risk to the balance sheet, and increases finance-expense volatility around refinancing events (e.g., the EUR300m note repurchase/reissue in HY26).

regulatory.description: Nearly all of Chorus' revenue and capex is determined by regulatory decisions (PQ2 covers 2025-2028); an adverse PQ3 (from 2029) determination on allowed WACC, RAB rollforward or expenditure allowances would directly cap future cash flows. The precise current RAB value and allowed WACC were not confirmed in the extracted filings and should be checked against the Commerce Commission's published PQ2 final determination and Chorus' CY25 Information Disclosure (due May 2026) before being used in valuation.

The Commerce Commission recommended deregulating copper services outside the fibre footprint in 2025/26 (citing FWA/satellite substitution), and Chorus has since brought forward full copper retirement from 2030 to 2028. This removes some regulatory certainty/TSO-style revenue on the shrinking copper base but also accelerates cost-out; net financial effect (write-offs vs. savings) is a swing factor to monitor through FY27-28.

The NZ Government announced in December 2025 that it would monetise (sell down) the National Infrastructure Funding and Financing Co (NIFFCo) debt/securities linked to the original UFB deployment (book value ~$642m); on 7 August 2026 Ministers announced the Crown had entered binding agreements to complete this monetisation for net proceeds of approximately $702m, with settlement expected during August 2026. Chorus has stated it does not anticipate material changes to the terms and conditions of the securities as a result, but NIFFCo will reportedly provide some (undisclosed) risk protection to the purchasers, which introduces a new institutional counterparty/structure around a meaningful slice of Chorus' balance sheet (Crown funding + NIFF securities totalled roughly $1.5bn of liabilities at 31 December 2025) and is worth monitoring for any indirect effect on Chorus' financing terms.

macro.description: Management has flagged a 'challenging' NZ economy; while broadband is a near-essential service, plan downgrades, slower new-connection growth, and payment difficulties among retail customers can flow through to Chorus.

As a highly-levered, long-duration infrastructure asset with a regulator-set allowed return, Chorus' equity value and dividend capacity are directly sensitive to the risk-free rate and the WACC the Commerce Commission allows in each regulatory period.
100% of revenue and assets are in New Zealand, with no geographic diversification to offset a domestic regulatory, macro or political shock.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: New Zealand's fixed broadband market is transitioning decisively to fibre (the dominant fixed technology per OECD data) with copper now being retired industry-wide by 2028 (accelerated from 2030); growth is now incremental uptake and ARPU mix-shift rather than network build, consistent with global post-UFB fibre telco peers.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Low-to-moderate — broadband is a near-essential utility service with sticky demand, but new connections/property development activity and discretionary plan upgrades are somewhat sensitive to the NZ economic cycle and housing market.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High — Chorus carries roughly NZ$3.3bn of debt (~4.5x net debt/EBITDA) and is valued substantially on dividend yield/regulatory WACC dynamics, making both its cost of capital and its equity valuation directly sensitive to NZ and global interest rates.
key_input_costs: Electricity (network power consumption, partly offset by copper withdrawal energy savings)
Labour and field service company contractor costs
Debt/interest costs on NZD, EUR and AUD borrowings
Network equipment and IT/cloud migration costs

recent_developments.event: NZ Finance Minister Nicola Willis and Infrastructure Minister Chris Bishop announced the Crown had entered binding agreements to monetise (sell down) the National Infrastructure Funding and Financing Co (NIFFCo) debt it holds in Chorus, originating from interest-free UFB loans made 2012-2023. Net proceeds to the Crown are reported at approximately NZ$702m (a ~$60m gain over the $642m book value); settlement expected during August 2026. Reporting indicates NIFFCo will provide purchasers some limited, undisclosed risk protection. Chorus stock was reported little-changed/slightly down on the news and Chorus has said it does not expect material changes to the terms of the underlying securities.

Chorus announced it would accelerate full retirement of the copper network to 2028, two years earlier than the prior 2030 target, following the Commerce Commission's 2025 draft/final recommendation to deregulate copper access services outside the fibre footprint on the basis that FWA and satellite competition has made copper regulation unnecessary; copper connection volumes have been falling sharply (reported double-digit percentage declines quarter-on-quarter in some periods).

HY26 EBITDA rose 3% to $357m (HY25: $346m); revenue $506m (HY25: $500m); net profit swung to $15m (from a $5m loss in HY25, which included accelerated depreciation on copper assets); fibre connections grew ~14,000 in the half to 1.129m (95% of the 1.192m total fixed-line connections); fibre uptake reached 72.4%; fibre ARPU rose to $57.73/month (Dec-24: $55.34); gross capex was $158m, down $41m half-on-half; interim dividend of 24 cents per share declared (up 4% YoY), paid 14 April 2026, no DRP available for the interim dividend; total equity fell to $430m at 31 Dec 2025 (from $567m at 30 June 2025).

NZ Government first announced its intention to commence a sale/monetisation process for the NIFFCo securities linked to the original UFB build; process concluded with the binding agreements announced August 2026 (above).

Chorus issued EUR400m of new medium-term notes (7-year, 3.529% coupon, fully hedged to NZD) and repurchased EUR243m of its EUR300m 2026-maturity notes at 81.5% of face value, refinancing/derisking a 2026 maturity ahead of time.

FY25 net profit returned to $4m (from a $9m FY24 loss); revenue $1.014bn; EBITDA $705m; full-year dividend of 57.5 cents (up 21% YoY, at the top end of the raised 70-90% net operating FCF payout range); fibre uptake reached ~72%.

Commerce Commission issued its final determination on Chorus' price-quality path for the second regulatory period (PQ2), covering 1 January 2025 to 31 December 2028, setting the expenditure allowances and revenue caps that now govern Chorus' regulated cash flows through FY2028.

Mark Aue (ex-2degrees CEO, ex-Vodafone NZ/One NZ CFO) became CEO, succeeding JB Rousselot who led Chorus through the completion of the UFB rollout; new CEO has driven an operating model change and organisational simplification (permanent/fixed-term headcount down from 849 to 751 between HY25 and HY26).

Board completed a capital management review, raising the dividend payout target to 70-90% of net operating free cash flow (after sustaining capex), up from 60-80% previously, reflecting greater post-UFB cash flow visibility; policy explicitly targets dividends that grow at the rate of inflation.

guidance.as_of: H1 FY2026 Results (23 February 2026); no update identified as of 10 August 2026

items.notes: Unchanged range but management guided to the upper half at the HY26 result; up from FY25 actual of $705m. No public update to this range identified since 23 February 2026; FY26 results are typically reported in late August and had not been released as of 10 August 2026.

Subject to no material adverse change in circumstances or outlook; up from 57.5 cents in FY25 (+4.3%). Interim dividend of 24 cents per share was paid 14 April 2026; dividend reinvestment plan was not available for the interim dividend.

Expected to land in the lower half of the range as fibre installation volumes and new-connection capitalised labour continue to taper post-UFB; HY26 gross capex was $158m, down $41m half-on-half, of which sustaining capex was $79m and discretionary growth capex $79m.

items.target: Not to materially exceed 4.75x in normal circumstances
items.notes: Internal tolerance level, with a buffer to the ~5.0x threshold typically cited by rating agencies; actual was approximately 4.5x at 31 December 2025.

Board considers a BBB-equivalent rating appropriate; rated BBB/positive outlook by S&P and Baa2/stable by Moody's as at the HY26 report (23 Feb 2026). No subsequent rating action identified as of 10 August 2026 -- confirm against current agency reports before relying on this for valuation.

Brought forward from the prior 2030 target (April 2026 announcement), following the Commerce Commission's recommendation to deregulate copper access services; copper cables/ducts/poles in Chorus' fibre-serviceable areas were already largely fully depreciated by mid-2026, with non-fibre areas now targeted for full depreciation/retirement by 2028 rather than 2030.

guidance.management_commentary: At the HY26 result, management reiterated confidence in the FY26 outlook, citing steady fibre connection growth (95% of connections now fibre), ARPU gains from the January 2025 price increase, and cost discipline from the copper withdrawal and organisational simplification programmes. FY26 EBITDA guidance was expected to land in the upper half of the $710-730m range, and the FY26 dividend of 60 cents per share was reaffirmed, subject to no material adverse changes in circumstances or outlook. CY25 RAB capex allocations remain unaudited pending the Information Disclosure announcement due in May 2026. Since the HY26 result, the main incremental news has been (i) the April 2026 decision to accelerate copper retirement to 2028, framed by management as both a customer-migration and cost-reduction opportunity, and (ii) the Crown's August 2026 monetisation of its NIFFCo loans to Chorus, which Chorus has characterised as not changing the terms of its own obligations. Full FY2026 results had not been published as of 10 August 2026 (Chorus typically reports in the second half of August).

bull_case: Regulated monopoly with multi-year revenue/cash-flow visibility under the PQ2 (2025-2028) framework, now largely past the heavy UFB build capex cycle, structurally expanding free cash flow

High and growing dividend (60 cents FY26 guidance, up from 42.5 cents FY22) under a payout policy (70-90% of net operating FCF) explicitly targeting inflation-linked growth — an attractive, relatively defensive income profile for an infrastructure/utility investor

Copper network withdrawal is a self-funding, now-accelerated (2028 vs prior 2030) cost-out programme: as the last fixed copper lines are retired, network maintenance, electricity and depreciation costs fall while fibre ARPU and margin rise
Fibre uptake still has room to run toward management's 80% target (72.4% at HY26), and gigabit/multi-gigabit plan mix-shift continues to lift ARPU even without further regulatory price increases

Improving credit profile (S&P outlook positive as of the HY26 report; leverage trending down from build-era peaks) creates optionality for either further deleveraging, incremental discretionary investment, or faster dividend growth
bear_case: High leverage (~4.5x net debt/EBITDA, and total equity down to $430m against ~$3.3bn of debt) leaves little room for a downside surprise (regulatory, rate, or EBITDA), and a large, EUR/AUD-denominated debt stack recurs through 2032, creating ongoing refinancing and interest-rate risk

Structurally capped upside — as a fully regulated wholesaler, Chorus cannot reprice or reallocate capital outside the Commerce Commission's PQ framework; the next reset (PQ3, from 2029) is a multi-year-out but material valuation swing factor, and the exact current RAB/allowed-WACC inputs need verifying against the Commerce Commission's own published determination rather than assumed

Fixed wireless (5G) and Starlink/LEO satellite are genuinely eroding the addressable market at the margin — the same substitution the Commerce Commission cited to justify copper deregulation is capping fibre's realistic uptake ceiling and threatening low-end ARPU/connections

Interest-rate sensitive equity valuation: as a high-payout, high-leverage bond-proxy stock, CNU is vulnerable to a higher-for-longer global rate environment compressing the relative attractiveness of its dividend yield; naive P/E screens are meaningless given near-zero reported net income (HY26 EPS $0.03) driven by heavy D&A and interest expense against a much larger EBITDA base

Government NIFFCo debt monetisation (binding agreements announced 7 August 2026, ~$702m proceeds to the Crown) is framed as immaterial to Chorus' own contractual terms, but introduces a new counterparty/protection structure around roughly $1.5bn of Crown-related liabilities on Chorus' balance sheet and keeps political/ownership-structure attention on the stock during 2026
